headline: Orbital torque from a thick titanium/tungsten bilayer writes a magnetic memory bit on 300-millimetre wafers for under 0.1 picojoule, removing the few-nanometre spin source that has capped the technology.

items.title: MRAM's torque layer gets thicker, and the write energy falls below 0.1 pJ
items.dek: Dinggui Zeng and colleagues built magnetic memory cells on 300-millimetre wafers whose switching torque comes from electron orbital motion in a thick titanium/tungsten bilayer rather than from spin in an ultrathin heavy metal, and report a 182 percent read signal with under 0.1 picojoule per write.
items.why_it_matters: Spin-orbit-torque cells have been stuck on a manufacturing problem rather than a physics one: the film that generates the torque has to be a couple of nanometres of tungsten or tantalum, and a film that thin varies across a wafer in a way that shows up directly as cell-to-cell variation in the current needed to flip a bit. Moving the effect to a light-metal orbital source lets that film be thick enough that thickness control stops being the limiting step, and it decouples the choice of conductor from the need for strong spin-orbit coupling — which widens the list of materials a memory array can be built from.
items.background_md: Magnetic memory stores a bit as the direction of magnetisation in a thin ferromagnet, read out through a tunnel junction whose resistance depends on whether two magnetic layers point the same way. Writing it means applying a torque. Spin-orbit torque does that by running current through an adjacent conductor: scattering inside heavy metals such as platinum, tantalum or tungsten separates electrons by spin, and the resulting spin current pushes on the magnet. The torque per unit current scales with spin-orbit coupling, which is why the field went to heavy elements — and heavy elements are exactly where the useful films are only a few nanometres thick.
items.deeper_md:
The orbital Hall effect is why a light metal can work at all: an applied field separates carriers by orbital angular momentum rather than by spin, and that separation does not require large spin-orbit coupling, so titanium — which has almost none — can be the source. The orbital current only becomes a torque once it is converted into spin inside a layer that does have coupling, which is what the tungsten half of the Ti/W bilayer is for.

The preprint's numbers are tunnel magnetoresistance of 182 percent, nanosecond response, 10¹² write cycles and under 0.1 pJ/bit on a 300 mm platform. For scale, Gupta and co-workers measured roughly 30 percent higher damping-like torque efficiency and about 20 percent lower switching current from a ruthenium orbital layer against platinum across more than 250 devices, so a whole-bilayer redesign producing a step in E_b/I_c sits on that trajectory rather than off it.

What the abstract does not give is the absolute switching current, the thermal stability factor behind E_b/I_c, or whether switching is field-free — and a cell that still needs an in-plane bias field is a different product from one that does not.

glossary.definition: A write mechanism that drives current through a conductor beside the magnet; spin-orbit coupling sorts the electrons by spin, and the resulting spin current exerts a torque that flips the magnetisation.
The percentage resistance difference of a magnetic tunnel junction between its parallel and antiparallel states; it sets how much signal the sense amplifier gets, so it decides the read margin.

Transverse separation of carriers by orbital angular momentum rather than by spin; it survives in light elements with negligible spin-orbit coupling, which is why titanium can act as a torque source at all.
Picojoules of energy spent writing one bit — the figure of merit that decides whether a non-volatile memory can sit next to a processor or has to live out at the storage tier.

items.fab_angle: A 2 nm tungsten film has to be controlled to a fraction of a nanometre across a 300 mm wafer, which makes it an X-ray-reflectivity and ellipsometry problem before it is a device problem. A torque source that works at ordinary sputtered thicknesses moves that burden off in-line metrology and onto target composition and chamber cleanliness instead.

items.title: The substrate decides which way ε-Ga₂O₃ polarises, and whether a channel forms
items.dek: Yan Wang, Zhigao Xie, Weihua Tang and Chee Keong Tan showed that growing the wide-bandgap oxide ε-gallium oxide on aluminium-polar aluminium nitride gives films whose built-in spontaneous polarisation points up, while growing it on sapphire points it down, and set out an atomic-stacking rule that tells you which one you have.
items.why_it_matters: Polarisation in a crystal is a vector, and its sign is not a detail: across a heterointerface it is the step in polarisation that supplies the bound sheet charge, so one orientation collects a conducting electron sheet and the reverse orientation depletes it. An earlier modelling study of ε-(Al,Ga)₂O₃ barriers put the charge ratio between those two cases above 1,600. Until now that sign could neither be chosen during growth nor read back off a finished film, which meant device stacks in this material were being drawn without knowing which side of that ratio a given wafer would land on.
items.background_md: Gallium oxide is a wide-bandgap semiconductor being developed for power switching. Its orthorhombic ε phase is also polar: the crystal carries a large built-in electric polarisation along one axis with no field applied. In a polar material, a change in polarisation from one layer to the next leaves uncompensated bound charge at the interface, and free electrons collect there as a two-dimensional sheet — which is how AlGaN/GaN transistors get a channel with no doping at all. The direction is fixed while the film grows, and it is not something an ordinary structural measurement hands back, because inversion-related structures scatter X-rays almost identically.
items.deeper_md:
The identification rule is geometric. ε-Ga₂O₃ is orthorhombic and non-centrosymmetric, and inside its stacking sits an asymmetric four-atom sequence; the authors assign polarity from the relative elevation of the atoms within that sequence, calibrated against interferometric piezoresponse on the same films. Epitaxy on aluminium-polar AlN reproduces the substrate's registry and gives uniformly Ga-polar films with polarisation pointing up; epitaxy on sapphire gives O-polar films pointing down. Let crystallinity degrade and the registry breaks, leaving mixed polarity inside one film — the failure mode that makes a device irreproducible rather than merely worse. It is the same substrate menu, sapphire and AlN among them, that Bhuiyan and co-workers used when mapping band offsets for this phase.

What the sign is worth was quantified earlier by Ranga and co-workers, who paired density-functional theory with a Schrödinger–Poisson solver on ε-Ga₂O₃/ε-AlGaO₃/ε-Ga₂O₃ double heterostructures and obtained charge contrast ratios above 1,600 between the normal and reversed cases.

Two caveats. This is a preprint, and the assignment rests on correlating a piezoresponse phase with an atomic model rather than on an independent absolute reference. And nothing here is a transistor: no sheet density, mobility or breakdown number is reported.

glossary.definition: A permanent electric dipole per unit volume that a non-centrosymmetric crystal carries with no applied field; its direction, not only its magnitude, follows from how the crystal is stacked.
A conducting electron sheet trapped against a heterointerface, a few nanometres thick, formed here by the bound charge left where polarisation changes between layers rather than by dopant atoms.
Which end of the polar axis faces out of the film. Inverting it flips the sign of the interface bound charge, so the identical layer stack either accumulates carriers or depletes them.
An atomic-force method that applies a voltage through the tip and measures the film's mechanical response; the phase of that response tracks the sign of the polarisation beneath it.

items.fab_angle: If polarity is inherited from the substrate, it becomes a purchasing decision as much as a recipe parameter: an AlN template and a sapphire wafer put through the same reactor recipe yield opposite devices, and a partially relaxed template yields both at once on one wafer.

items.title: A sweep of 1,000 point-adder designs shrinks the ZK proof engine threefold
items.dek: Gaurav Kuwar and four co-authors built a generator that sweeps more than 1,000 hardware variants of elliptic-curve point addition — the inner loop of zero-knowledge proof generation — and the best of them come out 2.71 times faster and 3.11 times smaller than hand-built 12-nanometre ASIC blocks.
items.why_it_matters: Accelerators for this workload are whole chips of a few hundred square millimetres — one published design takes 366 mm² and feeds itself 2 TB/s — so the area spent inside the innermost arithmetic block decides how many copies of it fit. The transferable result is not the speedup but which knob produced it: the winning configurations are single-precision and fully pipelined, while multi-precision variants, attractive because they reuse one narrow datapath over several passes, carry a latency penalty the authors call severe. That is a rule that applies to any wide-word modular arithmetic unit, proof system or not.
items.background_md: A zero-knowledge proof lets one party convince another that a computation ran correctly without revealing its inputs. Generating one is expensive, and nearly all of the cost sits in two primitives: the number-theoretic transform, and multi-scalar multiplication, which repeatedly adds points on an elliptic curve. One point addition is a fixed sequence of multiplications and additions modulo a prime several hundred bits wide. So the hardware question is always the same question — how to build a modular multiplier that wide, and how many of them the area budget allows.
items.deeper_md:
The axes Locus sweeps are the ones a hardware engineer would argue about: Montgomery against Barrett reduction; Karatsuba decomposition zero to four levels deep against schoolbook multiplication; word widths of 16, 32, 64 and 128 bits; whether the prime modulus and curve constants are folded in as constants or left variable; and two curve representations, Jacobian coordinates for short Weierstrass curves and extended projective for twisted Edwards. Designs come out of Catapult high-level synthesis and are scored in Design Compiler against a 12 nm GlobalFoundries library at 1 GHz.

Per-curve results run 1.67–3.32× faster and 1.91–3.30× smaller than prior ASICs. On an UltraScale+ FPGA the fastest configuration completes a point addition in 50 cycles at 291 MHz, or 0.172 µs. Dropped into existing accelerators at equal area, end-to-end proof generation improves 3.15× geomean.

The caveat the authors state themselves: their multi-scalar multiplication latency model assumes uniform scalars and simple scheduling, which is exactly where the clever bucket algorithms live. So of the three headline numbers, the end-to-end one rests on the most assumptions.

glossary.definition: Summing many elliptic-curve points, each first multiplied by its own scalar; it dominates proof-generation time, and every scalar multiplication decomposes into repeated point additions.

Arithmetic modulo a large prime done with shifts and multiplications instead of division, by working in a transformed representation; the alternative, Barrett reduction, precomputes a reciprocal instead.
Splitting a wide multiply into three half-width multiplies instead of four, recursively; it trades multiplier area for extra adders, and each level of recursion moves that trade further.
A projective way of writing elliptic-curve points that carries a third coordinate so each addition avoids a modular inversion, paying for it in extra multiplications.

items.fab_angle: The whole result is produced by high-level synthesis into a commercial standard-cell library and scored with a normal synthesis tool — the same flow a student team runs on an open PDK, with the generator rather than the schematic as the thing being designed.

items.title: KV cache traffic moves onto the mesh instead of through one port
items.dek: Dong Liu and Yanxuan Yu rebuilt the key-value cache of a tiled transformer accelerator as traffic on an on-chip mesh network — every cache block owned by one tile and fetched as routed packets rather than through a shared memory path — and measured 58 percent less interconnect traffic at 32,000-token context.
items.why_it_matters: Producing one token means reading every key and value produced before it, so bytes moved per token grow with how long the conversation already is while arithmetic per token does not. Serving software has attacked that by packing the cache more tightly in memory; this attacks the on-die half, where the constraint is not capacity but that many tiles want the same blocks in the same cycle through one injection point. Spreading ownership across tiles and multicasting a block to the tiles that asked for it converts a queue at a port into traffic on links that were sitting idle.
items.background_md: A transformer generates text one token at a time, and each new token attends to every earlier one. Rather than recompute the earlier keys and values, hardware keeps them — the key-value cache — and reads the whole thing back for every token produced. That makes generation bandwidth-bound rather than arithmetic-bound: the multiply-accumulate arrays wait on memory. On a tiled accelerator the compute is already spread across dozens of processing tiles joined by an on-chip network, but the cache has usually stayed one logical pool reached over a shared path, which turns the network into a funnel.
items.deeper_md:
MeshKV places macro-blocks by an affine map π(ℓ,s) = (ℓ mod W, (a·ℓ+s) mod H), with a coprime to the mesh height — the coprimality is what stops consecutive layers and sequences landing on the same row and recreating the hotspot. Blocks then reach consumers over multicast trees rooted at the owning tile, with exact-tag tables and Bloom filters suppressing duplicate copies of a head.

The prototype is an 8×8 mesh on an Alveo U280 with 512-bit wormhole links; each tile carries a systolic array at head dimension 128, 288 KB of KV SRAM in four banks, and a two-virtual-network router with eight-flit FIFOs. Against a round-robin-placement, unicast baseline it reports 2.1× better KV bandwidth utilisation and up to 1.9× multi-stream throughput at batch size 8, with decode latency growing roughly linearly in context length where the centralised design's growth is steep.

Two limits the authors state: only the communication substrate is built, not the feed-forward and normalisation layers, and absolute latencies are not comparable against other FPGA decoders on different parts.

glossary.definition: The stored keys and values of every token processed so far; it grows with context length, and reading it back each step is what makes generation memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

A network-on-chip scheme where a packet is cut into flits that stream through routers head-first without the whole packet being buffered, keeping router storage small at the cost of holding links during a stall.
A routing pattern that carries one copy of a block along shared links and forks it only where destinations diverge, instead of injecting an independent copy per consumer.
The fixed-size chunk a network-on-chip advances in one cycle; buffer depth is counted in flits, and it sets how much a router can absorb before it pushes back on its neighbour.

items.title: Where data lives becomes a type, and in-storage compute stops being hand-placed
items.dek: Yuyue Wang, Zhenyu Zhang, Glenn Reinman and Huaicheng Li gave an in-storage computing language three annotations — host memory, device memory, flash — so a programmer declares where a value lives rather than which processor runs each stage, and report 4.2 times the throughput of running the same pipelines on the host.
items.why_it_matters: Earlier in-storage systems made placement the programmer's job, which is why they handle one-stage scans and come apart on pipelines: a multi-stage job has intermediate results, and anyone who must say which processor computes each stage ends up hand-managing what survives between calls and what gets copied back out. Separating residency from execution lets the compiler derive those lifetimes instead — values scoped to one invocation die there, values explicitly kept become device-resident state — and it is the persistence primitive, not the placement annotation, that lets stage two consume stage one without a round trip through the host.
items.background_md: A solid-state drive moves far more data internally than it can present at its host interface, because the flash sits on several parallel channels that all funnel into one controller and one PCIe link. In-storage computing is the idea of running part of a query or a model inside the drive so only the answer crosses that link. The hardware already exists — drive controllers carry ARM cores, and research devices add accelerators. The standing obstacle is software: there is no ordinary way to express which part of a program runs where, so every system has invented its own.
items.deeper_md:
Epic's three location types are @host, @slm (the drive's own DRAM) and @flash, and they annotate residency only, not which unit executes. Lifetime falls out of that: values inside one invocation are CallState with compiler-derived lifetimes, while an epic.keep marks SharedState that survives across invocations — which is what lets an embedding table stay resident rather than being re-shipped every call.

The numbers are 4.2× over host execution across twelve workloads, up to 16.1× on a DLRM embedding lookup, 1.6× over the strongest of five prior in-storage systems reimplemented on the same reference device, and up to 14× less application code.

The caveat is the platform. That reference device — eight flash channels, eight ARM cores at 1.8 GHz, a four-tile NPU, eight near-flash processors at 800 MHz — is modelled in FEMU, a QEMU-based NVMe emulator whose own documentation notes the emulated device lives in memory, with gem5 and ONNXim supplying accelerator timing. These are projections, not measurements on silicon. The authors also scope the work to regular, read-heavy analytics and exclude graph traversal and write-heavy paths. A separate line of work, NITRO, attacks the same bottleneck in hardware by buffering intermediate activations in the drive's DRAM instead of programming them into TLC NAND.

glossary.definition: Running part of a computation on processors inside a storage device, so that a filtered or reduced result crosses the host link instead of the raw data.
One of several independent buses joining a drive's controller to its NAND packages; internal bandwidth is the sum across channels, which is how it comes to exceed what the host interface carries.

The gather step in a recommendation model that pulls a handful of rows out of a table far too large for accelerator memory; it is nearly pure random reads, which makes it the favourite in-storage benchmark.
A QEMU/KVM-based NVMe drive emulator from FAST 2018, used when the research device does not exist in silicon; its timings are modelled, so results obtained on it are projections.

items.title: Student and teacher disagree on how to stop, and the answers get longer
items.dek: Yuxiao Yang and eight co-authors traced runaway response lengths in on-policy distillation — training a small model on its own outputs graded by a larger one — to the two models putting their stopping probability on different end-of-sequence tokens, and fixed most of it by pooling those tokens into one stop action.
items.why_it_matters: The tokenizer is normally treated as settled plumbing, below the level at which training objectives get argued about. Here a lexical accident changes an optimisation: Qwen3's published generation config declares two valid stopping tokens, 151645 and 151643, and if the base model's mass sits on one while the instruction-tuned teacher's sits on the other, the update penalises the student every time it stops the way it knows how, while the alternative it is being pushed toward starts from a probability too small to reach by sampling. Any objective defined over tokens now needs a notion of which tokens mean the same thing.
items.background_md: A language model does not stop by running out of things to say; it emits a special end-of-sequence token, and the serving loop halts on seeing one from a declared set. Models usually declare several — a document-end marker inherited from pretraining, a turn-end marker added when the model became a chat assistant — and both are legal stops. On-policy distillation trains a student on text the student generated itself, scoring each sampled token by how much more probability the teacher would have put on it. The objective therefore works token by token, with no notion that two tokens can mean the same thing.
items.deeper_md:
The per-token signal is A_t = log π^E(y_t|s_t) − log π_θ(y_t|s_t): the student is pushed down on any sampled token the teacher likes less than it does. When the student samples its own preferred stop and the teacher's mass sits on a different but equivalent stop, that term is negative even though the teacher fully intended to terminate. The paper reports the teacher-preferred token can carry student probability around 10⁻¹¹, so sampling will never find it, and the suppression compounds: responses lengthen until they hit the generation budget, and the clipping ratio climbs.

The three families fail differently. Qwen3's base model concentrates on 151643 while the post-trained model prefers 151645. Llama 3.2's post-trained variant adds 128008 and 128009 to the base's 128001. Gemma 3 declares identical sets, 1 and 106, and still diverges by learned preference — which rules out a configuration bug as the whole explanation.

The authors are explicit that the fix is partial: a late-stage re-inflation shows up in K2-Horizon runs after the termination token has transferred, the experiments cover single-turn mathematics only, and template sensitivity was checked on three Qwen3 templates.

glossary.definition: A reserved token whose emission ends generation. A model may declare several and the serving loop stops on any of them, so two distinct tokens can express one decision.

Training a student on sequences it generated itself and grading them with a teacher, instead of imitating teacher-written text — done to close the gap between training text and what the student actually produces.
The fraction of generated responses that hit the maximum-length budget rather than stopping on their own; it is the measurable symptom that a model has lost its termination behaviour.
The training signal here: the teacher's log-probability of the sampled token minus the student's. Negative values push the student off tokens it weights more heavily than the teacher does.

foundations.subtitle: Growing crystal on crystal, then deliberately getting the atomic spacing wrong so that carriers move faster.
foundations.tldr: Epitaxy grows a new crystal layer that continues the lattice of the wafer beneath it, which means the new layer inherits the substrate's atomic spacing instead of its own. Grow a material whose natural spacing differs and the film is forced to stretch or compress to fit; that distortion reshapes the energy bands, and reshaped bands move electrons and holes faster. Every high-performance CMOS process for roughly two decades has put strain into the channel on purpose, and the entire engineering problem is how much you can impose before the lattice gives up and tears.

sections.heading: A film with no say in its own spacing
sections.body_md:
Start with the thing that makes epitaxy different from every other deposition. In sputtering or plasma CVD you land atoms on a surface and they stick roughly where they hit; the film is polycrystalline or amorphous, and nobody expects otherwise. In epitaxy you run hot enough — for silicon, roughly 900 to 1100 °C — that an arriving atom skitters across the surface long enough to find the lattice site the substrate underneath is offering. The film continues the substrate's crystal rather than starting its own.

That is the whole benefit and the whole constraint in one sentence. The benefit is a layer with the electrical properties you specify and the crystalline perfection of the wafer: a lightly doped epitaxial layer on a heavily doped substrate gives you an abruptness no diffusion step can produce, which is why power devices and latch-up-hardened CMOS are built on epi wafers. The constraint is that the film does not get to choose its in-plane spacing. It gets the substrate's.
sections.deeper_md: Two epitaxial regimes are worth separating. Homoepitaxy — silicon on silicon — is about purity and doping profile, and the numbers that matter are autodoping from the substrate and the transition width of the doping step. Heteroepitaxy is about mismatch, and it is where everything in this piece happens. A third mode, selective epitaxy, grows only on exposed silicon and not on oxide or nitride, by adding enough chlorine chemistry that nucleation on the dielectric is etched away as fast as it forms. Selective growth is what makes the source/drain stressors in section five possible at all: you need the film to appear in the recess and nowhere else.

sections.heading: Mismatch, and the thickness at which the lattice gives up
sections.body_md:
Silicon and germanium have the same diamond crystal structure and differ only in size: germanium's lattice constant is about four percent larger. Alloy them and you get an intermediate spacing, roughly linear in germanium fraction. Now grow silicon-germanium on a silicon wafer. In the plane of the wafer the film has to match silicon, so it is compressed; being compressed sideways it bulges vertically, and the unit cell goes from cubic to tetragonal. The film is now storing elastic energy, and the amount stored per unit area grows with thickness.

Somewhere there is a thickness at which it becomes energetically cheaper to give up: to insert a misfit dislocation at the interface, relieve the strain, and accept a line defect instead. That is the critical thickness, and it is the single number that governs strained-layer engineering. It falls fast as mismatch rises, because the stored energy per unit thickness goes as the square of the mismatch while the cost of a dislocation barely changes.
sections.deeper_md:
The classical criterion is Matthews and Blakeslee's force balance: the misfit stress acting on an existing threading dislocation versus the line tension resisting it, which gives a critical thickness that behaves like h_c ∝ (b/f)·ln(h_c/b) with b the Burgers vector and f the mismatch — implicit in h_c, which is why solutions get written with the Lambert W function.

AMD's US6943087B1 puts the practical numbers on it for strained silicon grown over a relaxed silicon-germanium buffer: about 20 percent germanium underneath supports roughly 200 Å of strained silicon before misfit dislocations become likely, while 30 percent germanium supports only about 80 Å. A 50 percent increase in germanium fraction costs you 60 percent of your usable thickness. Note also that Matthews–Blakeslee is an equilibrium criterion; films grown cold are routinely metastable and thicker than it allows, and they relax the first time somebody anneals them.

sections.heading: Why stretched silicon carries current better
sections.body_md:
Here is the part that is not obvious: pulling the lattice apart by well under one percent changes mobility by tens of percent. The mechanism is band structure, not geometry. Silicon's conduction band minimum is not one valley but six equivalent ones along the cube axes, and each valley is an ellipsoid — light effective mass in two directions, heavy in the third. In an unstrained crystal all six are at the same energy, so the electron population is spread across all of them and the average mass a transport calculation sees is a mixture.

Apply biaxial tension in the plane of the wafer and the six valleys stop being equivalent. Two drop in energy, four rise. Electrons redistribute into the lower two, which happen to present their light mass in the transport plane. Two things improve at once: the average conductivity mass goes down, and scattering between the two groups of valleys — which needs a phonon carrying enough energy to cross the new gap — becomes less likely.
sections.deeper_md:
The AMD patent states the effect as electrons "effectively weigh 30 percent less" in the lowered valleys, and claims potential mobility increases of 80 percent or more for electrons and 20 percent or more for holes. Note the asymmetry, because it drove the industry's next move: biaxial tension is good for electrons and much less good for holes, whose valence band is warped and degenerate in a way that biaxial tension does not cleanly split.

The same patent also asserts that electrons in strained silicon "scatter at a rate of 500 to 1000 times less than in relaxed silicon." Treat that the way you would treat any number in a patent's background section: it is advocacy, not measurement, and a scattering-rate reduction of three orders of magnitude is not consistent with a mobility gain of 80 percent. Patents are excellent primary sources for what was built and why; their background prose is not peer-reviewed.

sections.heading: The relaxed buffer, and the roughness it leaves behind
sections.body_md:
To stretch silicon you need something underneath with a larger spacing, which means you need silicon-germanium that has already relaxed to its own natural lattice constant. That is deliberate defect engineering: grow the germanium content up gradually over a micrometre or more so that misfit dislocations form at many different depths, and the threading segments that connect them have room to glide sideways and annihilate rather than piling up and threading into the surface. Then grow a few tens of ångströms of silicon on top, and it is in tension.

The buried dislocation network does not stay buried in its effects. Each misfit line locally relieves strain, and the surface above it dimples. The result is cross-hatch: a visible orthogonal pattern of ridges running along the two in-plane directions the dislocations prefer. You have bought mobility with a surface that is no longer flat and a strain field that is no longer uniform.
sections.deeper_md:
Peña and co-workers measured exactly this on 25 commercially grown Si₀.₇Ge₀.₃ heterostructure wafers with Raman microscopy and cross-sectional STEM, then fed the measured strain into a device model. Their finding is that cross-hatch strain variation implies spurious detunings of order 0.1 meV between two quantum dots 100 nm apart, and they report mean valley splittings of 70 ± 13 against 77 ± 14 µeV. Their recommendations are thicker virtual-substrate buffers and growth at or below 700 °C to limit strain-driven surface diffusion.

The relevance beyond qubits: a non-uniform strain field is a non-uniform threshold voltage. Cross-hatch is the reason biaxially strained silicon-on-relaxed-SiGe never became the mainstream logic answer despite winning on electron mobility — the substrate cost, the roughness, and the variation all landed on the same wafer.

sections.heading: Uniaxial strain: stress the channel, not the wafer
sections.body_md:
The approach that actually shipped in volume abandons straining the whole wafer and strains one transistor's channel instead, from the outside. Etch a recess where the PMOS source and drain will go. Refill it by selective epitaxy with silicon-germanium. The refilled material wants a larger lattice constant than the silicon around it, and it is clamped, so it pushes — and the silicon channel sitting between two such recesses is squeezed along the direction current flows.

Uniaxial compression along the channel is what holes want, which is precisely what biaxial tension failed to deliver. The knob is germanium fraction, and it has been turned steadily: Intel's patent on strain-inducing source/drain regions notes that 30 percent germanium gives a lattice constant about one percent above silicon's, a GlobalFoundries patent reports 30 percent embedded silicon-germanium producing about 50 percent more strain than 20 percent, and a 2025 Intel patent describes filling the recess with more than 50 percent germanium.
sections.deeper_md:
The competing constraint is contact resistance, and it pulls the same knob in the opposite direction at the surface. The GlobalFoundries patent reports that 20 percent embedded silicon-germanium has two to three times the contact resistance of 30 percent, and then describes stacking alternating high- and low-germanium layers so that the silicide consumes only a thin sacrificial low-germanium cap and leaves the thick high-germanium stressor intact. That is the real shape of the problem: the stressor, the silicide and the dopant activation are all competing for the same volume of material.

The 2025 Intel patent is explicit that low-germanium source/drain structures "do not necessarily provide added strain to a SiGe channel" — once the channel itself contains germanium, a 20 percent stressor is no longer pushing on anything.

sections.heading: Strain is a budget, and it is spent early
sections.body_md:
Two habits of mind are worth taking away. First, strain is a one-time gain, not a scaling law. Dennard scaling gave you a better transistor every node for free; strain gave you one better transistor, once, and everything since has been about not losing it. That is why the germanium fraction keeps climbing — it is the only direction left on that particular knob.

Second, strain is stored energy, and every hot step after the stressor is deposited is an opportunity for the lattice to spend it. Dopant activation anneals, silicide formation, contact and interconnect processing all sit downstream of the source/drain epitaxy, and every one of them is bounded partly by a relaxation risk rather than by diffusion alone. The thermal budget argument that governs the back end of the line has a front-end twin, and it is this one: a metastable strained film survives until somebody heats it.
sections.deeper_md: A useful way to hold all of this at once is to notice that three different failure modes are all the same physics seen from different angles. Exceed the critical thickness and you nucleate misfit dislocations. Relax a graded buffer and you get cross-hatch and threading dislocations at the surface. Anneal a metastable stressor and you lose the stress you paid for. In each case the system is trading elastic energy for defect energy, and the only variables are how much mismatch you imposed, over what thickness, and how much thermal energy you subsequently supplied to let it find the lower state.

glossary.definition: Deposition hot enough that arriving atoms find lattice sites and continue the substrate's crystal rather than forming their own, so the grown film is single-crystal and registered to what is beneath it.
The fractional difference in natural atomic spacing between film and substrate, (a_film − a_sub)/a_sub. Silicon to germanium is about 4 percent; Si₀.₇Ge₀.₃ on silicon is about 1 percent.

The film thickness above which relieving strain by nucleating a misfit dislocation costs less energy than continuing to store it elastically. It falls steeply with mismatch, and it is an equilibrium criterion that cold-grown films routinely exceed.

A misfit dislocation lies in the interface plane and is what actually relieves strain; a threading dislocation is the segment that runs up through the film to the surface, and it is the one that kills devices.

A thick, compositionally graded silicon-germanium layer grown until it relaxes to its own lattice constant, so that silicon grown on top of it is in tension. It is bought at the price of cross-hatch roughness.

The orthogonal ridge pattern a relaxed graded buffer leaves on its surface, each ridge sitting above buried misfit dislocations that locally relieve strain. It makes both the surface height and the strain field non-uniform.
Silicon-germanium grown selectively into etched source/drain recesses so that its larger lattice constant squeezes the channel between them, giving uniaxial compression along the current direction.

Silicon's conduction minimum is six equivalent ellipsoidal pockets. Biaxial tension splits them into two lower and four higher; electrons crowd into the lower two, which present their light effective mass in the plane of transport.

foundations.try_this: Pull US6943087B1 and US7629603B2 from Google Patents — both are free and both have readable background sections — and read them side by side. One builds biaxial tension from a relaxed silicon-germanium buffer, the other builds uniaxial compression from recessed source/drain epitaxy, and between them they carry the two numbers that decide the trade: roughly 200 Å of usable strained silicon over 20 percent germanium versus about 80 Å over 30 percent, and roughly 1 percent lattice mismatch for Si₀.₇Ge₀.₃. Then do the arithmetic they leave out. Take germanium's lattice constant as about 4 percent above silicon's, assume Vegard's law, and compute the mismatch for 20 and 30 percent germanium; check that the ratio of the two critical thicknesses the patent quotes is steeper than 1/f, which tells you the dislocation-energy term is doing work too. If you want the third pass, note that the 900–1100 °C window silicon epitaxy runs in overlaps the range the club's tube furnace covers — which is the fastest way to feel why anything strained has to survive every thermal step that comes after it.
